terms.def: Attacking the person instead of the argument. A fallacy.
A good result of the affirmative's plan; a policy case usually has one to three.
The side that supports the resolution. Also called pro, proposition or government in some formats.
In Congress, the first speech on a piece of legislation, given by its author (or a sponsor), followed by a longer questioning period.
The form a judge fills out with the winner, speaker points and the reason for the decision.
In British Parliamentary debate, the two teams on the same side: the government bench or the opposition bench.
A prepared set of answers to an argument you expect. In policy, "the negative block" also means the back-to-back 2NC and 1NR.
The point at which a disadvantage's harm is about to happen; the reason the plan would push things over the edge.
The duty to prove a claim. The side asking the judge to accept something new usually carries it.
Each side's duty to answer the other side's arguments; an unanswered argument may be treated as true.
A quoted piece of evidence with its tag and full citation.
A side's prepared opening speech: its framework and main arguments.
The group of students debating together in a Congress session.
The source information for a card: author, qualifications, date, title, publication and page or URL.
The point an argument makes, stated in a sentence.
Direct engagement between the two sides' arguments. Judges reward rounds where debaters answer each other.
Claiming to read parts of a card you actually skipped. A serious ethics violation.
In British Parliamentary debate, the second pair of teams on each bench (closing government and closing opposition).
In Public Forum, the toss that decides which team picks its side or its speaking order.
Narrowing to your best one or two arguments in the final speeches.
The requirement that a counterplan give a reason to reject the plan, usually because doing both is impossible or worse.
To agree with or not contest an argument, on purpose or by not answering it.
A speech that builds a case; the first speeches in most formats.
One main argument in a case, with its claim, warrant, evidence and impact.
A negative's alternative to the affirmative plan that it argues is better. Often called a CP.
In Lincoln-Douglas, the standard for measuring whether the value is achieved. Also called the value criterion or standard.
Public Forum's questioning periods, in which both debaters ask and answer.
A period in which one debater questions another. Often called CX.
To boil the round down to its key issues in a final speech.
Preparing evidence: choosing a passage, writing a tag, adding the cite, and highlighting what you'll read.
The meaning a side gives to a key word in the resolution, ideally from a reliable source.
In British Parliamentary debate, the second speaker of an opening team (Deputy Prime Minister or Deputy Leader of the Opposition).
A Congress questioning style in which one questioner gets a short segment (often 30 seconds) for back-and-forth questions.
A negative argument that the plan causes a harm, with uniqueness, a link and an impact. Often called a DA.
Sharing which arguments you've run so future opponents can prepare; common on some circuits.
Changing a quotation's meaning by adding or removing words. A serious ethics violation.
The list of legislation a Congress chamber will debate.
An argument the other side never answered. Point it out and extend it.
A round after the preliminary rounds in which the loser leaves the tournament. Also called an outround.
Aristotle's word for a speech argument that starts from what the audience already accepts and often leaves a step unstated.
Persuasion through the speaker's character as shown in the speech: good sense, good character and good will.
A phrase that shows your argument wins under the other side's assumptions too ("even if they're right about cost, we outweigh").
Facts, data, expert testimony or examples that support a claim.
A speech event in which students answer a current-events question after 30 minutes of preparation. Often called extemp.
To carry an argument into a later speech by restating its claim, warrant and impact.
In British Parliamentary debate, the new line of argument a closing team must add.
A mistake in reasoning that can make a weak argument look strong.
The last two-minute speech for each team in Public Forum.
Notes taken in columns, one per speech, so arguments and answers line up. Also a verb: to flow a round.
An experienced judge who keeps a detailed flow and decides from it.
A way to answer any argument: they say, but, because, therefore.
The standard a side asks the judge to use in deciding the round.
Prepared answers that defend your own case against expected attacks.
A few seconds allowed to finish a sentence after time runs out, set by each tournament.
Public Forum's three-minute questioning period with all four debaters.
The arguments each side can fairly make under a resolution or definition.
The problem in the present system that the affirmative plan aims to solve.
Why an argument matters: who is affected and how much.
Arguing that the result the other side calls bad is actually good (or the reverse).
Speaking with only a few minutes to prepare.
Why the present system won't solve the problem on its own.
An argument that challenges the assumptions or language behind the other side's case. Often called a K.
A judge without debate experience, such as a parent or community member.
The first opposition speaker in parliamentary formats.
A bill or resolution debated in Congress.
The connection showing that a plan or position causes a particular result.
Arguing that the plan actually causes the opposite of what the other side claims.
Persuasion through argument and evidence.
Winning the round while receiving fewer speaker points than the losing side.
How big an impact is. One of the main ways to weigh.
In British Parliamentary debate, the first speaker of a closing team.
The topic in parliamentary and World Schools debate, often "This House would..."; also a procedural request in Congress.
The side that opposes the resolution. Also called con or opposition.
An answer saying the harm will happen anyway, with or without the plan.
A first-year or beginning debater; many tournaments have novice divisions.
Negative positions that aren't direct answers to the affirmative's case, such as disadvantages and counterplans.
Arguments that answer the affirmative's case directly.
In British Parliamentary debate, the first pair of teams on each bench.
The posted list of who debates whom, where, on which side and with which judge.
A judge's statement of how they judge, often posted online.
Persuasion through the listeners' emotions, fairly used when tied to real impacts.
The specific policy the affirmative proposes to carry out the resolution.
A short question or statement offered during the other side's speech, outside protected time; the speaker may accept or decline. Often called a POI.
In parliamentary debate, an objection that the other side has made a new argument in a rebuttal.
In Congress, the rule that students who have spoken less are called on first.
One of the rounds every entry debates before elimination rounds. Often called a prelim.
Time each side may use during the round to prepare its next speech.
The student elected to run a Congress session. Often called the PO.
The side the judge favors if neither side proves its case; in policy debate, traditionally the negative.
The first government speaker in parliamentary formats.
Reading an argument in its most reasonable form; the idea behind steelmanning.
How likely an impact is to happen. One of the main ways to weigh.
The first and last minute of a speech, when points of information may not be offered.
In Congress, the time after a speech when other legislators ask questions.
The judge's explanation of why one side won. Often called the RFD.
To defend your own arguments after the other side attacks them.
A speech that answers the other side, defends your case and sums up. Also any answer to an argument.
In Congress, the rule that, among students who have spoken equally often, the one who spoke longest ago is called on first.
Showing that an argument is wrong or doesn't matter.
In World Schools debate, the four-minute summary given by each side's first or second speaker, opposition first.
The statement being debated, often beginning "Resolved:".
Whether an impact can be undone. Irreversible harms are often weighed more heavily.
A short preview of the order of your speech, given before the clock starts in many leagues.
A tournament in which every team debates every other team.
Telling the judge where you are in your speech ("On their first contention...").
Whether the plan actually solves the problem.
A score for each debater's speaking and argument, separate from the win.
Speaking very fast to fit more arguments in; accepted by some judges and not others.
The way things are now, without the proposed change.
The other side's argument restated in its strongest form; also the verb for answering that version.
The classic parts of a policy case: harms, inherency, plan and solvency (and often topicality).
A distorted, weaker version of someone's argument, built to be knocked down. A fallacy.
The third speech for each team in Public Forum, which narrows the round to key issues.
The tournament office that pairs rounds, collects ballots and tallies results.
A card's one-line summary, written by the debater.
A short, memorable name for a contention, easy for a judge to write down.
Arguments about what debaters should be allowed to do, such as which counterplans are fair.
How soon an impact happens. One of the main ways to weigh.
Whether the affirmative's plan fits the resolution's words. Often called T.
Showing that the other side's argument actually supports your side.
Showing that a harm isn't happening now and would happen only because of the plan.
In Lincoln-Douglas, the highest goal the round should be judged by, such as justice. Also called the value premise.
The main reasons a debater gives the judge to vote for them, usually in the last speech. Also called voting issues.
The reason a claim is true; what connects the evidence to the claim.
Comparing impacts to show the judge why yours matter more, using magnitude, probability, timeframe and reversibility.
In British Parliamentary debate, the last speaker on each bench, who sums up without new arguments.
